A model that predicts well has not thereby explained anything. It has found patterns that are
useful for prediction, which may be causal, may be proxies, and may be artefacts of how the
data were collected. A habitat model can achieve excellent accuracy by learning where the
survey vessels went.

This final section is about the step between having a model and making a scientific claim:
which features actually drive the predictions, whether an interpretable model would serve you
better than an accurate black box, how to report the work so that someone else could repeat
it, and how to be straight about uncertainty.

Because the survey is simulated, every claim on these pages can be checked against what was
actually put into the data. Several of them fail that check, and those are the useful ones.

:::

## What this section found

- Three columns of `rnorm()` noise ranked **sixth, seventh and eighth of sixteen** on the
  default impurity importance — above salinity, above `survey_year`, and above every
  substrate term, on every split we tried. Substrate has a real effect; the noise does not.
- Across eight splits of the same data, chlorophyll's permutation-importance rank ran from
  **first to eleventh**. The only two predictors that never beat a noise column were salinity
  and `survey_year` — which are exactly the two with no effect in the generator.
- The true depth response peaks at 80 m. A random forest's partial dependence declines
  monotonically; so does a negative-binomial GLM given the generator's **exact** functional
  form, which estimates the depth quadratic at a fourteenth of its true value with
  $p = 0.63$. Accumulated local effects give the same answer.
- Individual-station curves for temperature have humps between 1.35 and 5.98 counts tall,
  peaking anywhere from 6 °C to 11.75 °C. **The average of them is shorter than any one of
  them.**
- On identical folds the **GAM beat the random forest and the boosted trees** — RMSE 4.08
  against 4.28 and 4.74 — closing 83% of the gap between a no-skill baseline and an oracle.
  It also recovered the substrate ordering and salinity's null effect, which the importance
  measures got wrong.
- Changing the random forest's seed moved the test RMSE by **0.016**. Changing which rows
  were held out moved it by **1.50**.
- A 95% confidence band on the mean covered **29%** of the observed counts. An interval built
  from a forest's in-sample RMSE covered 77%. Conformal prediction covered 96.5% — at
  constant width, with a lower bound of −9.1 animals.

::: {.callout-important}
**No interpretation method recovers an effect the data does not identify.** Depth and
temperature are confounded by this survey's design — there are almost no cold shallow stations
and almost no warm deep ones — and every method here reports the same wrong depth response as
a result. The GAM is the only one that also reports that it does not know: its interval covers
the true curve at 197 of 200 grid points and excludes zero only below 155 m. A
partial-dependence plot has no mechanism for saying "the data cannot answer this".
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**And one error defeats every safeguard in this course.** If the gear recovers only half the
animals on rock, the recorded counts on rock are halved, the estimated rock effect more than
doubles — from "38% fewer than gravel" to "69% fewer" — and the biased model's cross-validated
RMSE and R² both *improve*. Resampling compares a model against the data, so a bias in the
data passes every check. The defences are gear calibration, an independent method and
transparent reporting of effort. None of them is a model.
:::
